passage: Tuesday. Chemistry again. I understood nothing of balancing equations, and half the class was finishing early. Jagdish Sir said, “Doubt? Come to my room at lunch.” I nodded and didn't go. If I go, he'll think I'm not clever enough, and Ritu, who sits ahead of me, will know. So I sat with the book in the library, drawing arrows. I've been doing this for three weeks. It's stupid. The next test is Friday, and I know I will fail equation balancing. My stomach is a stone. Asking feels like admitting I'm the weak one. But not asking has cost me everything I've tried. Maybe tomorrow I'll go to his room. Maybe. — Arohi

qa.q: Where did Jagdish Sir ask Arohi to come at lunch?
qa.a: Jagdish Sir asked Arohi to come to his room at lunch.

qa.q: Why did Arohi not go to Jagdish Sir's room?
qa.a: Arohi felt ashamed and afraid of being judged, sure that asking would mean admitting to being the weak one.

qa.q: What could Arohi do about the Friday test?
qa.a: Go to Jagdish Sir's room at lunch tomorrow with one specific equation and ask how to balance it.

qa.q: How might Jagdish Sir see students who do not come to his room?
qa.a: Jagdish Sir probably wants to help and would be glad to see Arohi, and may think a doubt is a normal thing to bring.

grounding: A teenager struggles alone with a subject because asking feels like admitting failure among peers who seem to understand.

passage:
Kamal: are you going to ask Ma'am about the pendulum problem?
Jeevan: no
Kamal: it's been three weeks, you keep saying you'll get it
Jeevan: everyone else gets it. if I ask it looks like I've been sleeping in class 😶
Kamal: no it doesn't. I asked about circuits last month
Jeevan: you're smart, it's different
Kamal: I'm not smart, I asked. that's the whole difference
Jeevan: hm
Jeevan: what if she says “you should know this by now”
Kamal: then you'll know she said it, and you still get the answer. coming to her table with me tomorrow?
Jeevan: ...maybe

qa.q: How many weeks has Jeevan been stuck on the pendulum problem?
qa.a: Jeevan has been stuck on the pendulum problem for three weeks.

qa.q: What is Jeevan afraid of about asking Ma'am?
qa.a: Jeevan is afraid of looking like someone who was sleeping in class and worries that Ma'am might say “you should know this by now”.

qa.q: What did Kamal say and do that made the request feel possible?
qa.a: Kamal shared having asked about circuits, said “I asked, that's the whole difference”, and offered to go to Ma'am's table together.

qa.q: How might Kamal feel about Jeevan's replies?
qa.a: Kamal is probably patient and caring, gently answering each fear while hoping Jeevan will say yes.

grounding: A teenager struggles alone with a subject because asking feels like admitting failure.

passage:
Charu: "Pradeep, your chemistry marks dropped again. What's going on?"
Pradeep: "Nothing. I'll figure it out."
Charu: "You said that last month. Why don't you ask Iyer sir?"
Pradeep: "And have the whole class watch me ask what moles are? In Class Eleven?"
Charu: "Half of them don't get it either."
Pradeep: "They look like they do."
Charu: "Looking isn't understanding. You've been stuck for six weeks."
Pradeep: (quiet) "Asking feels like admitting I'm not good enough for science."
Charu: "Asking is how you get good enough. Go to the staffroom after school. No one's watching there."
Pradeep: "What do I even say?"
Charu: "Say, 'I don't understand moles. Can you explain from the start?'"
Pradeep: (sighs) "Fine. Tomorrow."

qa.q: How long had Pradeep been stuck in chemistry?
qa.a: Pradeep had been stuck for six weeks.

qa.q: What was Pradeep afraid of if he asked Iyer sir?
qa.a: Pradeep was afraid it would look like admitting to not being good enough for science, especially in front of classmates who seemed to understand.

qa.q: What small step did Charu suggest, and why could it work?
qa.a: Going to the staffroom after school with one simple sentence, so Pradeep could ask without an audience.

qa.q: How might Charu see Pradeep's six weeks of silence?
qa.a: Charu sees it as avoidable struggle caused by pride and fear, and pushes Pradeep kindly toward asking.

grounding: A dialogue shows a teenager struggling alone for weeks because asking a teacher feels like admitting failure.

passage: I'm Yamini, and in Class Ten I nearly failed accounts because I was too proud to ask. I'd always been a topper in maths, so when ledgers stopped making sense, I couldn't admit it. My friend Sarika would ask the teacher questions in class without blinking, and I thought, she's brave, or she doesn't care what people think. Every evening I stared at the balance sheet, trying to force it. For five weeks. My marks slid from 90 to 58. Finally Sarika dragged me to the teacher at lunch. It took the teacher ten minutes to fix what had confused me for five weeks. I walked out embarrassed, and so relieved I almost laughed.

qa.q: How far did Yamini's marks slide?
qa.a: Yamini's marks slid from 90 to 58.

qa.q: What was Yamini afraid of that stopped the asking?
qa.a: Yamini felt too proud and afraid to admit struggling, having always been a topper in maths.

qa.q: What lesson could Yamini take from the ten-minute fix?
qa.a: Asking early costs a few minutes of embarrassment, while silence cost five weeks and a big drop in marks.

qa.q: How might Sarika see asking questions in class?
qa.a: Sarika seems comfortable and unbothered, seeing questions as normal rather than a sign of weakness.

grounding: A teenager recalls struggling alone for weeks because asking for help felt like admitting failure.

passage:
Maths teacher's note, Class 9, after the monthly test.
Yusuf scored 34, far below his usual. In class he never asks questions and nods whenever I check. After the test I asked him to stay. At first he said the test was just hard. Then he admitted he had been lost since the chapter on algebraic identities, three weeks ago. "Everyone else seems to get it," he said. "I didn't want to look dumb." His classmate Jyoti, waiting outside, told me later that he had been copying her homework. I have set up a short doubt session twice a week at lunch, open to all, so asking doesn't single anyone out. Yusuf came to the first one today.

qa.q: What score did Yusuf get on the test?
qa.a: Yusuf scored 34.

qa.q: Why had Yusuf stayed silent in class?
qa.a: He was embarrassed and afraid of looking dumb, since everyone else seemed to understand.

qa.q: Why is the open lunchtime session a wise response?
qa.a: Because it is open to all, asking doesn't single anyone out, which lowers the fear of judgment.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel about Yusuf copying her homework?
qa.a: Jyoti might feel uneasy and a bit worried for him, which may be why she told the teacher.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a teenager who hid his confusion for weeks rather than ask for help in front of classmates.

passage:
Thursday
Five weeks now of pretending I understand trigonometry identities. Today Mrs Pillai asked the class, "Who wants to come to the doubt session at lunch?" Three people raised their hands. Jeevan didn't need to, obviously; Jeevan finishes the worksheet before she's done writing it on the board. I kept my hands flat on the desk. If I go, everyone will know the "bright one" can't do sin and cos.
So instead I spent two hours tonight on videos and got more confused. Got 9 out of 25 on the class test. Mum saw it and asked why I never ask for help. I said I'm figuring it out.
Am I, though? Five weeks. If I'd gone in week one it would probably be sorted by now.
Maybe tomorrow at lunch. Maybe.
Trisha

qa.q: How many people raised their hands for the doubt session?
qa.a: Three people raised their hands.

qa.q: Why did Trisha keep both hands flat on the desk?
qa.a: Trisha was afraid of being judged and too proud to let the class see the "bright one" struggling, so staying still felt safer.

qa.q: What small step could Trisha take tomorrow?
qa.a: Go to the lunch doubt session with one written question, or ask Mrs Pillai privately before class, so the first ask is short and less public.

qa.q: If you were Mrs Pillai, what would you want Trisha to know?
qa.a: That the doubt session is exactly for this, that asking is not failing, and that five weeks of struggle could have been a few minutes of help.

grounding: Shows a teenager who struggles alone for weeks because asking the teacher in front of capable peers feels like admitting failure.
